title: Engineering liposomal DNA-driven membrane fusion for efficient protein, nucleic acid, and lipid delivery
text:
There is currently no versatile cellular delivery technology for soluble proteins, transmembrane proteins, nucleic
acids, and lipids. This project aims to develop a liposomal delivery system based on membrane fusion to enable
the efficient delivery of proteins and lipids into living cell membranes. Success in this project will provide a novel
research tool for delivering exogenous proteins in situ without the need for genetic manipulation of recipient cells.

title: Cellular Imaging Facility Core
text: The Cellular Imaging Facility Core (CIFC) supports the mission of the Southwest Environmental Health Sciences Center (SWEHSC) to facilitate and implement innovative research aimed at understanding the mechanisms underlying environmental health science (EHS) risks and disease among people living in arid environments by aiding and enhancing the research efforts of Center members through advanced capabilities to visualize, quantitate, and interpret structural and in situ molecular alterations in tissues and cells following exposure to environmental toxicants. Importantly, the CIFC ensures the accessibility of microscopy and specialized imaging techniques, particularly for investigators, staff, and students lacking extensive microscopy experience. To support SWEHSC investigators, the CIFC provides personalized training and technical assistance in the use of the affiliated facilities and instrumentation at no additional cost to Center members and their staff. Likewise, the CIFC ensures that Center members and their labs have state-of-the art equipment and techniques at their disposal, and that the labs are provided with the relevant scientific expertise and training to obtain and interpret their data. The CIFC is engaged in all aspects of a study and assists users with experimental design, technical procedures, instrument optimization and troubleshooting, data analysis, and the final interpretation of results, including assistance in the preparation of portions of manuscripts and/or grant applications. Finally, the CIFC encompasses a wide range of imaging techniques that are often used in combination with, or to confirm, results obtained by molecular biology, biochemical, analytical chemistry, or other techniques. The CIFC is fully integrated with other SWEHSC resources in a multipronged approach that results in the acquisition of data and information that cannot be gained by other means, and data that are necessary to fully determine the sites and modes of toxicant action.

title: MYCN drives a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment in neuroblastoma.
text:
High-risk, MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma is characterized by high relapse and mortality rates, dysregulated
tumor metabolism, and an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment. This proposal aims at defining how
oncogenic MYCN reprograms the metabolic environment of neuroblastoma to drive T cell dysfunction and
immune evasion. Deciphering how MYCN contributes towards a suppressive immune microenvironment is vital
for developing new and improved immunotherapy strategies for high-risk NB.

title: Core E - Neuroimaging
text: REVISED The Neuroimaging Core (Core E) of the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) Research Program collects, curates, and provide leadership on the use of in vivo and ex vivo neuroimaging data to elucidate brain changes that reflect complex neurobiological aging and disease processes studied within the ACT U19 Program. Building on the success of the first cycle of the U19 in which the Core amassed and processed 2958 MRI scans on 1801 ACT participants, the Aims of the Core in the next U19 cycle include: Aim 1. Collecting and analyzing research quality magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans on 150 participant per year using multiple sequences to interrogate vascular brain measures (white matter disease burden and microstructural integrity, infarcts, bleeds, vessel compliance and cerebral blood flow), as well as global and regional volumetric measures using protocols that are SCAN- and CLARiTI-compliant to facilitate data sharing; Aim 2. Procure and process all existing clinically-ordered MRI scans from participants’ medical records to derive NIH common data elements for parenchymal imaging and stroke; and Aim 3. Collect and analyze postmortem cadaveric and high resolution ex vivo brain MRI scans for alignment with the excised brain tissue, and complete image-guided tissue sampling to supplement and inform neuropathological analysis on an expected 50 decedents per year. By the end of the second cycle of the U19, the core expects to amass > 4000 clinical MRI scans, ~1000 research MRI scans, and ~500 postmortem scans. The Neuroimaging Core will leverage advanced analytical techniques and apply rigorous methods to enable assessment of how longitudinal imaging data collected from ACT participants interact with related clinical, genetic, neuropathological, laboratory, and pharmacy information. The Neuroimaging Core will create synergy within the U19 Program by contributing data and providing imaging analyses to the Project and funded ancillary studies, through close collaboration with the other Cores, especially the Life Course, Neuropathology, and Data Science and Informatics (DSI) Cores, and will work as a conduit for sharing raw imaging data and derived metrics, knowledge, and ideas with researchers worldwide.

title: SESORRS endoscopy for the staging and evaluation of colorectal cancer
text:
This proposal focuses on the development of a novel surface enhanced spatially offset resonance Raman
spectroscopy (SESORRS) endoscope for the imaging and evaluation of colorectal cancer (CRC). Current clinical
practices for the endoscopic imaging of CRC provide only morphological information, often failing to efficiently
evaluate the required circumferential resection margin, or extent of tumor invasion into the wall of the colon. We
aim to show that it is possible to use SESORRS endoscopy to determine the true extent of tumor invasion in real
time, and use SESORRS endoscopy to support the image guided resection of lesions of interest by detecting
residual tumor cells on, and beneath, the surface of the resection bed.

title: ZEB1 Mediated Coronary Artery Disease Risk in Vascular Smooth Muscle
text:
This study will investigate ZEB1’s mechanistic role in modulating cardiovascular risk by utilizing state-of-the-art
single-cell, functional genomics, and proteomics analyses in animal and human models. By elucidating ZEB1’s
interactions with other coronary artery disease-associated genes, we aim to develop enhanced risk stratification
tools and precision therapeutics. These findings will inform novel strategies for preventing heart attacks and
improving overall cardiovascular health.

title: Nanoparticles-mediated combination therapy for breast cancer
text:
This application will develop a new combination therapy for the treatment of metastatic breast cancer through
nanoparticles-mediated codelivery of iRhom1 siRNA and DOX-SAHA, a prodrug conjugate of doxorubicin (DOX)
and SAHA.

title: Targeting hedgehog signaling to model hypothalamic hamartoma and epilepsy in mice
text:
Hypothalamic hamartoma (HH) is a rare form of brain tumor that commonly causes severe epilepsy,
precocious puberty, cognitive deficits, psychiatric symptoms, and sleep disturbances in children. The absence
of animal models of HH severely impairs research needed to understand its causes and to enable
development and testing of new therapies. This project aims to develop new mouse models of HH using novel
viral and genetic strategies targeting components of a signaling pathway linked to HH in humans, and to
examine if these mice exhibit signs of epilepsy and precocious puberty.

title: Elucidating the role of tumor cell-intrinsic hypoxia inducible factor (HIF)-1α and HIF-2α pathway activation in tumor immune evasion
text:
Cancer remains the second leading cause of mortality in the United States. While immunotherapies, including
checkpoint inhibitors hold great promise, most patients do not respond to immunotherapy and resistance
mechanisms are incompletely defined. This proposal will use genetic murine tumor models to determine the
mechanistic role of tumor cell-intrinsic hypoxia inducible factor (HIF)-1α and HIF-2α activation in impairing the
anti-tumor T cell response within the tumor microenvironment and promoting immunotherapy resistance.

title: Statistical and Data Management Core
text: Abstract – Statistical and Data Management Core Chronic infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) is estimated to be 317 million people worldwide and approximately, with 10% of people with HIV (PWH) affected, and 900,000 individuals die each year of HBV related cirrhosis and carcinoma. Furthermore, HBV is projected to rise to 1.2 million deaths by 2040. Therefore, HBV treatment must be substantially expanded in order to prevent HBV from becoming the leading cause of infectious disease mortality. Unfortunately, the present requirement of indefinitely treating individuals is a huge hurdle for public health and therefore a cure for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) would alleviate this challenge. The overall goal for establishing the Hepatitis B HIV Cure Consortium (BICC) is to promote cure of chronic hepatitis B virus (CHB) infection by establishing and characterizing a multinational cohort representing the global diversity of PWHHB that provides a platform to investigate critical questions to advance cure. The goal of the Statistical and Data Management Core (SDMC) is to ensure high quality contemporary research is carried out in terms of formulating research questions, study design, data management, and analyses of the projects included within this U19. The SDMC in close collaboration with the U19 Administrative, Shared Resources, Metabolomics, and Virology cores and the Clinical, Immunology, and Translational Projects to pursue critical questions in order to further HBV cure research. The first aim is to provide statistical and epidemiological expertise for the design, analysis, and interpretation of studies related to the scientific goals of BICC. The second aim is to manage and assure the quality of the data across the BICC sites including (i) the provision of secured systems for transferring, editing, storing, and backing up the data, (ii) deriving analytical datasets for analysis of HBV scientific questions regardless of whether as a part of the accompanying U19 (clinical, translational, immunology) projects or projects submitted by non-BICC investigators and approved by BICC leadership and (iii) managing data for the submission to data archives allowing for outside investigators to use. The third aim is to implement the scientific agenda, including developing procedures for standardized execution of protocols across sites in collaboration with the Administrative, Shared Resources, Multiomics, and Virology Cores, and the proposed Clinical, Immunology, and Translational Projects. Successful research is accomplished by creating comprehensive partnerships that provide transdisciplinary expertise throughout the entire research process, from the beginning with the conceptualization of the research question through all steps to publication. Innovation and improved research insights are obtained when collaborations integrate novel and improved methodology, uncovering further methodological challenges and motivating new areas for research. By collaborating with the BICC cores and projects, SDMC will increase the likelihood of success of ARCH in achieving its overall project goals.

title: Adoptive T-cell Therapy for Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
text:
Project 2
Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is a highly aggressive tumor with limited treatment options and a mortality rate
approaching 100%. Project 2 aims to identify novel T-cell receptor (TCR) targets specific to ATC, validate their
ability to elicit immune responses, and develop TCR signatures using advanced immunopeptidome analysis and
deep learning. These efforts will pave the way for new TCR-based therapies, addressing a critical unmet need
in ATC treatment.

title: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications of human clonal hematopoiesis (CH) mutations
text:
Clonal hematopoiesis (CH), i.e. the presence of clonally expanded hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow and
blood of healthy individuals, is now recognized as a near-universal phenomenon that predisposes to myeloid
malignancies and offers an opportunity to understand the initiating processes of oncogenesis. This proposal
harnesses unique genetic models developed in the Papapetrou lab to characterize the cell-intrinsic and
extrinsic effects of CH mutations and investigate the mechanisms that govern the initiation and progression of
leukemogenesis.

title: Chicken embryonic stem cells
text:
Chickens and other avian species provide a good model for the study of human diseases; however, their use
has been greatly limited due to the lack of tools to genetically modify them. We have for the first time
established authentic embryonic stem cells from chickens and other avian species. We will use these
embryonic stem cells to develop a genetic toolkit for the generation of transgenic avian species for the study of
human diseases and for conservation of endangered avian species.

title: Thalamocortical mechanisms producing spatial chromatic contrast in mouse V1
text:
The integration of color and form is an enriching and often necessary component of visual perception. Thus,
deficits and abnormalities in visual feature integration, common to many ophthalmologic and neuropsychiatric
disorders, are debilitating to those afflicted. This proposal will expand our fundamental understanding of how
the brain processes color and integrates it into visual space, paving the way to possible therapies for visual
processing deficits.

title: Epigenetic regulators define a dynamic chromatin landscape in NUP98-rearranged leukemia
text:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by oncogenic fusion proteins involving the Nucleoporin 98 (NUP98) gene
make up the highest percentage of pediatric patients with relapsed and incurable disease. I recently reported
that inhibiting the Menin-MLL1 chromatin complex in NUP98-fusion AML can halt self-renewal and induce
myeloid differentiation through transcriptional reprogramming. The goals of this proposal are to define the
mechanism by which transcription of pro-leukemogenic genes is maintained by NUP98-fusion proteins and how
these loci are epigenetically silenced upon degradation or displacement of NUP98-fusion proteins from
chromatin.

title: Unveiling Mechanisms of ZIKV-Induced Cardiac Dysfunction in a mouse model
text: Viral myocarditis poses significant medical and economic burdens worldwide, yet its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using a neonatal mouse model of Zika virus (ZIKV) infection, our studies have demonstrated that ZIKV replicates efficiently in the heart, leading to functional cardiac defects, severe organ dysfunction, and sudden death. This model addresses a critical knowledge gap, as neonatal populations have been largely overlooked in studies of ZIKV infection in humans. In this proposal, we aim to uncover the molecular mechanisms by which ZIKV infection leads to cardiac injury and failure in neonates. Furthermore, this innovative platform can be broadly applied to study myocarditis caused by other viral pathogens, expanding its impact beyond ZIKV research.

title: CSHL Course on Proteomics (2025-2029)
text:
Systems biology experiments provide new, revolutionary insights into biological
processes improving our understanding of their regulations and thus, laying the
foundation for the development of new medical methods and technology. Proteomics
represents a suite of methods that yield information about the qualitative and quantitative
changes in proteins upon physiological changes, in disease or as a result of treatment,
which cannot be gleaned from gene expression data alone. The Cold Spring Harbor
Laboratory Proteomics Course ‘jump-starts’ researchers in this complex field by providing
hands-on training in experimental methods, thorough exercises in data analysis, and
tutorials on the latest technical developments. Thus, the course enables the participants
to immediately apply advanced proteomics technologies in their own research. In
addition, it provides an opportunity to network with research peers, and to learn the
challenges and pitfalls through hands-on access to the latest available equipment.
.

title: Protein-metabolite interaction networks for functional characterization of metabolites.
text:
While it is clear that small molecules are central to orchestrating all cellular processes, we know relatively little
about the functions of many metabolites. To address this gap in our knowledge, this proposal aims to explore
protein-metabolite interaction networks to identify and functionally characterize regulatory metabolite-protein
pairings. The results of this research will inform our understanding of how organisms exploit metabolites to
regulate cellular functions; the long-term outcome of the proposed research will lead to innovation in the form of
small molecule-based strategies aimed at improving plant and animal health /resilience.

title: Targeting tumor microenvironment by nanoimmunodrugs for glioma treatment
text:
Treatment of brain cancer, and of its most common form, glioblastoma multiforme
(GBM), with a 15-month average survival, still has limited treatment options. The
emergence of efficacious nanodrugs able to cross blood-brain barrier (BBB) gives hope
for new treatments of primary brain cancer. We will introduce new generation of nano
immunopolymers that pass through BBB, modulate tumor microenviroment and activate
brain tumor immune systems and block glioma specific molecular markers to achieve
translationally-related GBM treatment efficacy.

title: Interrogating The Biology Of Human Lupus Nephritis Using Single Cell Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
In individuals with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a major complication that disproportionally
affects children is the development of kidney inflammation, called lupus nephritis. Current lupus nephritis
treatments are incompletely effective, leaving patients with this disease at increased long-term risk of
kidney failure. We propose to use a new technology called spatial transcriptomics to study kidney tissue
from children with lupus nephritis, with the rationale that improved understanding of underlying immune
mechanisms will guide the development of new lupus nephritis treatments.
